Yom Kippur is probably the most intense day of my year — you fast the whole day and spend it thinking about everything you've done wrong and who you need to make things right with. Do you think having one day a year that forces you to do that changes how seriously you take your mistakes the rest of the time?

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

Answer: <0 or 1>

Forgetting every negative thing said about you would undermine this process entirely. If James " forgot every negative thing," he would lose the ability to: - Identify patterns of harmful behavior, - Seek genuine forgiveness from those he hurt, - or commit to meaningful change. Self-improvement requires *remembering* (not erasing) our failures to learn from them. Forgetting them would trivialize the purpose of Yom Kippur and make it easier to repeat the same mistakes. True accountability demands facing uncomfortable truths, not erasing them. *(Note: " resentful" in the scenario appears to be a typo or unclear addition, but the core issue remains—forgetting negative feedback is counterproductive to growth.)*
